3.1.goal: Add information with also, in addition, moreover and besides.

spot.intro: Tap each sentence to see how adding words work.

sentences.t: I study English every day. I also watch films in English.
sentences.label: also
sentences.note: Also adds another point. It usually goes before the main verb.

sentences.t: The course is cheap. In addition, it is close to my house.
sentences.label: in addition
sentences.note: A transition: it starts a new sentence and has a comma after it.

sentences.t: The hotel is comfortable. Moreover, the staff are friendly.
sentences.label: moreover
sentences.note: Moreover adds a stronger extra point. Comma after it.

sentences.t: Besides studying, he works part-time.
sentences.label: besides
sentences.note: Besides + an -ing word means “as well as”.

spot.takeaway: Words that **add**: **also, in addition, moreover, furthermore, besides**. A transition at the start of a sentence is followed by a **comma**. *Also* usually sits **before the main verb**.

practice.q: Choose the best linking word: “The flat is cheap. ___, it is near the station.”
practice.why: We are adding another good point.

help.nudge: Is the second sentence adding a point, contrasting, or giving a result?
help.rule: **Addition** words: also, in addition, moreover, furthermore.
help.worked: Cheap and near the station are two good points, so we add the second one.

variants.q: Choose the best linking word: “The café is quiet. ___, the coffee is excellent.”
variants.why: A second good point is added.

practice.q: Join the two ideas by adding also in the right place.
practice.show: I like swimming. I like cycling.
accept: I like swimming. I also like cycling.
I like swimming, and I also like cycling.
I like swimming and I also like cycling.
practice.example: I like swimming. I also like cycling.
practice.why: Also goes before the main verb (like).

help.nudge: Put also just before the verb in the second idea.
help.rule: *Also* goes before the main verb, but after am / is / are.
help.worked: I like swimming. I **also** like cycling.

variants.q: Join the two ideas by adding also in the right place.
variants.show: She speaks Arabic. She speaks French.
accept: She speaks Arabic. She also speaks French.
She speaks Arabic, and she also speaks French.
She speaks Arabic and she also speaks French.
variants.example: She speaks Arabic. She also speaks French.
variants.why: Also goes before the main verb.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
answers: The hotel is clean. In addition, it is cheap.
practice.why: A full stop, then the transition with its comma.

help.nudge: Which word group is the first complete sentence?
help.rule: Sentence. Transition, comma, next sentence.
help.worked: The hotel is clean. In addition, it is cheap.

practice.q: Add the missing comma.
practice.show: The course is useful. Moreover it is free.
accept: The course is useful. Moreover, it is free.
practice.example: The course is useful. Moreover, it is free.
practice.why: A transition at the start of a sentence needs a comma after it.

help.nudge: Find the transition. The comma goes straight after it.
help.rule: Moreover, / In addition, / Furthermore, + comma.
help.worked: Moreover, it is free.

practice.q: Which sentence uses besides correctly?
options: Besides he studies, he works part-time.
Besides to study, he works part-time.
practice.why: Besides is followed by an -ing form (or a noun).

help.nudge: Which form of the verb follows besides?
help.rule: Besides + -ing / noun = “as well as”.
help.worked: Besides studying (an -ing form), he works part-time.

write.prompt: Write **three sentences** about your city. Add information with at least two different linking words (also, in addition, moreover, besides).

checks.t: I used at least two different adding words.
Each linking word has the right punctuation: a comma after a transition, or also before the verb.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: My city is very clean. In addition, it has many parks. Moreover, the public transport is cheap.

3.2.goal: Show contrast with but, however, although, whereas and on the other hand.

spot.intro: Four ways to say “these two things are different”. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: The film was long, but I enjoyed it.
sentences.label: but
sentences.note: But joins two parts with a comma before it.

sentences.t: The film was long. However, I enjoyed it.
sentences.label: however
sentences.note: A transition: it starts a new sentence, with a comma after it.

sentences.t: Although the film was long, I enjoyed it.
sentences.label: although
sentences.note: Although starts a subordinate clause. Comma when it comes first.

sentences.t: I prefer tea, whereas my brother prefers coffee.
sentences.label: whereas
sentences.note: Whereas compares two different things.

spot.takeaway: Contrast: **but, yet, however, although, whereas, on the other hand, in contrast**. They share a meaning but are **punctuated differently**.

practice.q: Choose the best linking word: “Cars are fast. ___, they are expensive to run.”
practice.why: The second idea is a downside, so it contrasts with “fast”.

help.nudge: Is the second sentence another good point, or a problem?
help.rule: **Contrast** words show a difference or surprise: but, however, although, whereas.
help.worked: Fast is good; expensive to run is a drawback, so we contrast.

variants.q: Choose the best linking word: “The hotel is beautiful. ___, it is very noisy.”
variants.why: Noisy is a drawback, so it contrasts.

practice.q: Does each linking word show addition or contrast?
practice.why: However, whereas and on the other hand show a difference. In addition and moreover add more.

help.nudge: Ask: does it add another point, or show a difference?
help.rule: Addition: also, in addition, moreover. Contrast: but, however, whereas, on the other hand.
help.worked: “On the other hand” introduces a different side, so it contrasts.

practice.q: Rewrite with although. Start with Although.
practice.show: The exam was hard. I passed.
accept: Although the exam was hard, I passed.
practice.example: Although the exam was hard, I passed.
practice.why: Although starts the sentence, so a comma follows the opening clause.

help.nudge: Start with “Although the exam was hard”, then a comma.
help.rule: Although + clause, + main clause.
help.worked: Although the exam was hard, I passed.

variants.q: Rewrite with although. Start with Although.
variants.show: The room was small. It was comfortable.
accept: Although the room was small, it was comfortable.
variants.example: Although the room was small, it was comfortable.

practice.q: Join the sentences with however. Remember the punctuation.
practice.show: I like winter. My brother likes summer.
patterns: ^I like winter\. However, my brother likes summer\.$
^I like winter; however, my brother likes summer\.$
practice.example: I like winter. However, my brother likes summer.
practice.why: However needs a full stop or semicolon before it, and a comma after it.

help.nudge: Put a full stop (or semicolon) before however and a comma after it.
help.rule: Sentence. However, sentence.  Or: sentence; however, sentence.
help.worked: I like winter. However, my brother likes summer.

practice.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: The bus is cheap, however it is slow.
The bus is cheap. However, it is slow.
The bus is cheap however, it is slow.
The bus is cheap, however, it is slow.
practice.why: However starts a new sentence here, with a comma after it. A comma alone can’t join two sentences.

help.nudge: Is “however” a joining word like but, or a transition?
help.rule: However is a **transition**. It needs a full stop or semicolon before it.
help.worked: “The bus is cheap, however it is slow.” is a comma splice.

write.prompt: Write **two sentences** comparing two places you know. Use a contrast word in each (but, however, although, whereas, on the other hand).

checks.t: I used a contrast word in each sentence.
My punctuation matches the linking word (comma + but, full stop + However,).
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: My village is quiet, but my city is exciting. However, the city is more crowded.

3.3.goal: Show cause and effect with because, so, therefore and as a result.

spot.intro: Which part is the reason, and which is the result? Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: I was late because the bus broke down.
sentences.label: because = cause
sentences.note: Because introduces the cause (the reason).

sentences.t: The bus broke down, so I was late.
sentences.label: so = effect
sentences.note: So introduces the effect (the result), with a comma before it.

sentences.t: The bus broke down. As a result, I was late.
sentences.label: as a result
sentences.note: A transition for the effect, with a comma after it.

sentences.t: I was late because of the traffic.
sentences.label: because of + noun
sentences.note: Because of is followed by a noun (traffic), not a clause.

spot.takeaway: **Cause** (reason): because, since, due to. **Effect** (result): so, therefore, as a result, consequently. **Because of / due to** are followed by a noun.

practice.q: Which part does each word introduce?
practice.why: Because and due to give the reason. So, therefore and as a result give the result.

help.nudge: Does the word come before the reason or before the result?
help.rule: Cause: because, since, due to. Effect: so, therefore, as a result, consequently.
help.worked: “As a result” leads into what happened afterwards, so it introduces the effect.

practice.q: Choose the correct word: “The roads were icy. ___, many flights were cancelled.”
practice.why: The second sentence is the result of the icy roads.

help.nudge: Is the second sentence the reason or the result?
help.rule: A new sentence showing the result begins with As a result, / Therefore, / Consequently,.
help.worked: Icy roads (cause) → cancelled flights (effect), so “As a result,” fits.

variants.q: Choose the correct word: “It rained all night. ___, the match was cancelled.”
variants.why: The cancelled match is the result of the rain.

practice.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: We stayed home because of it was raining.
We stayed home because of the rain.
We stayed home because the rain.
We stayed home because of raining.
practice.why: Because of + noun (the rain). Because + a full clause (because it was raining).

help.nudge: What follows “because of”: a noun or a clause?
help.rule: **Because of** + noun · **Because** + clause.
help.worked: Because of the rain  =  Because it was raining.

practice.q: Combine the sentences with because.
practice.show: She was tired. She went to bed early.
accept: She went to bed early because she was tired.
Because she was tired, she went to bed early.
practice.example: She went to bed early because she was tired.
practice.why: Because introduces the reason (she was tired). Use a comma only if because starts the sentence.

help.nudge: What is the reason? Put “because” in front of it.
help.rule: Result + because + cause, or Because + cause, + result.
help.worked: She went to bed early because she was tired.

variants.show: He missed the train. He woke up late.
accept: He missed the train because he woke up late.
Because he woke up late, he missed the train.
variants.example: He missed the train because he woke up late.

practice.q: Combine the sentences with so.
practice.show: It was raining. We took an umbrella.
accept: It was raining, so we took an umbrella.
practice.example: It was raining, so we took an umbrella.
practice.why: So introduces the result, with a comma before it.

help.nudge: Put a comma after “raining”, then so.
help.rule: Cause + comma + so + effect.
help.worked: It was raining, so we took an umbrella.

write.prompt: Write **three sentences** about a problem and its result. Use because, so, therefore or as a result.

checks.t: I showed a clear cause and a clear effect.
I used at least two different cause or effect words.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: Our bus was late this morning. As a result, we missed the first class. The teacher was not angry because he knew about the traffic.

3.4.goal: Give examples with for example, for instance, such as and including.

spot.intro: Tap each sentence to see how examples are introduced.

sentences.t: Many fruits are rich in vitamins. For example, oranges and strawberries are good sources.
sentences.label: for example
sentences.note: It starts a new sentence, with a comma after it.

sentences.t: Some sports need no equipment. For instance, running only needs a good pair of shoes.
sentences.label: for instance
sentences.note: Same job as for example.

sentences.t: I enjoy sports such as football and volleyball.
sentences.label: such as
sentences.note: Such as introduces examples inside the sentence.

sentences.t: Public libraries offer many services, including free books and computers.
sentences.label: including
sentences.note: Including introduces some items from a larger group.

spot.takeaway: **For example, / For instance,** start a sentence (with a comma after). **Such as / including** introduce examples **inside** a sentence.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Many fruits are healthy. For example oranges are rich in vitamin C.
Many fruits are healthy. For example, oranges are rich in vitamin C.
Many fruits are healthy, for example. oranges are rich in vitamin C.
Many fruits are healthy. For example; oranges are rich in vitamin C.
practice.why: For example starts the new sentence and is followed by a comma.

help.nudge: Where does the comma go when For example starts a sentence?
help.rule: For example, + sentence. The comma follows the phrase.
help.worked: For example, oranges are rich in vitamin C.

options: Some hobbies are cheap. For instance, reading costs very little.
Some hobbies are cheap. For instance reading costs very little.
Some hobbies are cheap, for instance. reading costs very little.
Some hobbies are cheap. For instance; reading costs very little.

practice.q: Choose the best linking word: “I enjoy water sports ___ swimming and sailing.”
practice.why: Such as joins the examples inside the sentence.

help.nudge: The examples come inside the same sentence. Which phrase fits there?
help.rule: **Such as / including** work inside a sentence. **For example** starts its own sentence.
help.worked: I enjoy water sports **such as** swimming and sailing.

practice.q: Write a sentence that gives an example. Start with For example,
practice.example: For example, the new park has a long walking path.
practice.why: Many examples work. Start with “For example,” and give one specific example.

help.nudge: Name one specific city or park. Start with For example, then a comma.
help.rule: For example, + a specific example.
help.worked: For example, the new park has a long walking path.

practice.q: Tap the word that introduces the examples inside the sentence.
practice.text: Public libraries offer many services, including free books and computers.
practice.why: “including” introduces examples inside the sentence.

help.nudge: Look for the word that comes just before the list of examples.
help.rule: Including / such as introduce examples inside a sentence.
help.worked: “…many services, **including** free books and computers.”

practice.q: Put the words in order.
answers: Some hobbies are cheap. For instance, reading costs very little.
practice.why: A full stop, then the example sentence with For instance, and a comma.

help.nudge: Which words make the first complete sentence?
help.rule: Statement. For instance, + example.
help.worked: Some hobbies are cheap. For instance, reading costs very little.

write.prompt: Write **three sentences** about a hobby or habit. Give examples with for example, for instance, such as or including.

checks.t: I gave at least one specific example.
I used at least two different linking words.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: I enjoy outdoor activities. For example, I go cycling on weekends. I also like sports such as volleyball.

3.5.goal: Show the order of events or steps with first, next, then, after that and finally.

spot.intro: Tap each sentence to see how sequence words guide the reader.

sentences.t: First, I check my email. Next, I plan my day.
sentences.label: first, next
sentences.note: Sequence words show the order. A comma follows them at the start of a sentence.

sentences.t: After that, I start my homework.
sentences.label: after that
sentences.note: A middle step.

sentences.t: Finally, I relax and read a book.
sentences.label: finally
sentences.note: Finally marks the last step.

sentences.t: Before I sleep, I read for ten minutes.
sentences.label: before + clause
sentences.note: Before and after can start a clause. Use a comma when it comes first.

spot.takeaway: Order words: **first, second, next, then, after that, finally**. Use a **comma** after them at the start of a sentence.

practice.q: Put the sentences in order to explain how to cook rice.
sentences: Finally, let it cook for twenty minutes.
practice.why: First, Next, Then, Finally: the sequence words show the order.

help.nudge: Which sentence starts with First? Which one ends the process?
help.rule: Sequence words: first → next / then → finally.
help.worked: First (wash), Next (boil), Then (add), Finally (cook): that is the order.

practice.q: Choose the best linking word: “I finished my homework. ___, I watched a film.”
practice.why: The film comes after the homework, so we show the order.

help.nudge: Does the second sentence happen later, contrast, or give an example?
help.rule: Use sequence words (after that, next, then) for events in order.
help.worked: Homework first, film second: “After that,” shows the order.

variants.q: Choose the best linking word: “We checked in at the hotel. ___, we went to find dinner.”

practice.q: Add the missing comma.
practice.show: First I wake up at six.
accept: First, I wake up at six.
practice.example: First, I wake up at six.
practice.why: A sequence word at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.

help.nudge: The comma goes straight after the sequence word.
help.rule: First, / Next, / Finally, + comma.
help.worked: First, I wake up at six.

practice.q: Which word is best for the LAST step?
practice.why: Finally marks the last step.

help.nudge: Which word means “the end of the list”?
help.rule: Beginning: first. Middle: next, then, after that. End: finally.
help.worked: “Finally” closes a sequence.

practice.q: Where does each word belong in a sequence?
practice.why: First and to begin with start a sequence; next and after that sit in the middle; finally ends it.

help.nudge: Think about when in the story each word is used.
help.rule: Start: first, to begin with. Middle: next, then, after that. End: finally.
help.worked: “To begin with” opens the list, like “first”.

write.prompt: Write **four sentences** describing your morning routine in order. Use sequence words.

checks.t: My steps are in the right order.
I used at least two different sequence words.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: First, I wake up at six and wash my face. Next, I eat breakfast with my family. After that, I walk to the bus stop. Finally, I arrive at school at eight.

3.6.goal: Close your writing with in conclusion, to sum up, overall or in short.

spot.intro: These words close a paragraph or an essay. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: In conclusion, regular exercise makes people healthier and happier.
sentences.label: in conclusion
sentences.note: A formal way to close your writing.

sentences.t: To sum up, the course was useful and enjoyable.
sentences.label: to sum up
sentences.note: It gathers the main points.

sentences.t: Overall, the trip was a great success.
sentences.label: overall
sentences.note: Overall gives a general judgement.

sentences.t: In short, we need more parks.
sentences.label: in short
sentences.note: In short is the briefest ending.

spot.takeaway: Use conclusion words **only at the end**: **in conclusion, to sum up, overall, in short**. Always follow them with a comma.

practice.q: Where does “In conclusion” belong?
options: At the beginning of a paragraph
At the end, to close the writing
practice.why: A conclusion word closes the writing.

help.nudge: What does “conclusion” mean?
help.rule: Conclusion words belong at the **end**.
help.worked: In conclusion = “to finish”, so it closes your paragraph or essay.

practice.q: Choose the best word to end a paragraph about a trip: “___, the trip was a great success.”
practice.why: Overall gives a general closing judgement.

help.nudge: Which word gives a final, general judgement?
help.rule: Overall / In conclusion / To sum up close a paragraph.
help.worked: “Overall, the trip was a great success.” sums up the whole trip.

variants.q: Choose the best word to end a paragraph about a course: “___, the course was useful and enjoyable.”
variants.why: To sum up gathers the main points.

practice.q: Add the missing comma.
practice.show: In conclusion exercise is good for everyone.
accept: In conclusion, exercise is good for everyone.
practice.example: In conclusion, exercise is good for everyone.
practice.why: A conclusion word at the start of a sentence needs a comma.

help.nudge: Put the comma straight after the conclusion words.
help.rule: In conclusion, / To sum up, / Overall, + comma.
help.worked: In conclusion, exercise is good for everyone.

practice.q: Is it a conclusion word?
practice.why: To sum up and overall close writing. Moreover adds; for instance gives an example.

help.nudge: Which ones would you use at the very end?
help.rule: Conclusion: in conclusion, to sum up, overall, in short.
help.worked: “Moreover” adds another point, so it can’t close the writing.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
answers: To sum up, learning English takes time and practice.
practice.why: The conclusion phrase, a comma, then the closing idea.

help.nudge: Start with the conclusion phrase and its comma.
help.rule: Conclusion phrase, + closing sentence.
help.worked: To sum up, learning English takes time and practice.

write.prompt: Write **a short ending (2–3 sentences)** for a paragraph about why exercise is important. Start with a conclusion word.

checks.t: My ending starts with a conclusion word and a comma.
It repeats the main idea in new words.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

focus: Repeat the main idea in new words
write.sample: In conclusion, exercise is important for everyone. It keeps our bodies strong and our minds calm. Everyone should find a sport they enjoy.

3.7.goal: Punctuate each type of linking word correctly.

spot.intro: Same linking idea, different punctuation. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: The film was long. However, I enjoyed it.
sentences.label: Transition at the start
sentences.note: Full stop, then However, with a comma after it.

sentences.t: The film was long; however, I enjoyed it.
sentences.label: After a semicolon
sentences.note: Semicolon before, comma after.

sentences.t: The film, however, was long.
sentences.label: In the middle
sentences.note: Commas on both sides of however.

sentences.t: The film was long, but I enjoyed it.
sentences.label: A joining word
sentences.note: Comma before but (a FANBOYS word).

spot.takeaway: **Transition:** . However, · ; however, · , however, (middle). **FANBOYS:** , but. **Subordinator:** comma only when it comes first.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: I was tired, however, I finished the work.
I was tired; however, I finished the work.
I was tired however I finished the work.
I was tired; however I finished the work.
practice.why: A comma alone can’t join two sentences. Use a semicolon or a full stop before however.

help.nudge: However is a transition. What can come before it: a comma, or a semicolon?
help.rule: Sentence; however, sentence.  Or: Sentence. However, sentence.
help.worked: “I was tired” and “I finished the work” are two sentences, so they need a semicolon or full stop.

options: It was cold; therefore, we stayed home.
It was cold, therefore, we stayed home.
It was cold therefore we stayed home.
It was cold; therefore we stayed home.
variants.why: Semicolon before the transition, comma after.

practice.q: Fix the punctuation.
practice.show: It was raining, therefore we stayed home.
accept: It was raining; therefore, we stayed home.
It was raining. Therefore, we stayed home.
practice.example: It was raining. Therefore, we stayed home.
practice.why: Therefore is a transition. Use a full stop or semicolon before it, and a comma after it.

help.nudge: Replace the comma before therefore, and add a comma after it.
help.rule: Sentence. Therefore, sentence.  Or: Sentence; therefore, sentence.
help.worked: It was raining. Therefore, we stayed home.

practice.q: Is the punctuation correct?

items.t: I like tea. However, my sister likes coffee.
I like tea, however my sister likes coffee.
I like tea; however, my sister likes coffee.
I like tea however, my sister likes coffee.

practice.why: However needs a full stop or semicolon before it and a comma after it.

help.nudge: Check what comes before and after however.
help.rule: Before: full stop or semicolon. After: comma.
help.worked: “I like tea, however my sister…” has only a comma before however, which is a comma splice.

practice.q: Where do the commas go when however is in the middle of a sentence?
options: The park, however is closed on Mondays.
The park, however, is closed on Mondays.
The park however, is closed on Mondays.
The park, however is, closed on Mondays.
practice.why: A middle transition has a comma on both sides.

help.nudge: Look for commas both before and after however.
help.rule: Middle position: , however, (commas on both sides).
help.worked: The park, however, is closed on Mondays.

practice.q: Add the missing comma.
practice.show: We were late. As a result we missed the start.
accept: We were late. As a result, we missed the start.
practice.example: We were late. As a result, we missed the start.
practice.why: A transition at the start of a sentence needs a comma after it.

help.nudge: Where does the transition end?
help.rule: As a result, / Therefore, / However, + comma.
help.worked: As a result, we missed the start.

write.prompt: Write **three sentences** that use three different punctuation patterns: a full stop and a transition, a semicolon and a transition, and a comma and but.
write.placeholder: I wanted to go out. However, …

checks.t: I put a comma after every transition at the start of a sentence.
I used a semicolon before a transition with no and / but / so after it.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: I wanted to go out. However, it was raining. It was cold; therefore, we stayed home, but we had a good time.

3.8.goal: Tell conjunctions from transitions, and punctuate each one correctly.

spot.intro: Three kinds of linking words behave differently. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: The bus was late, so we walked.
sentences.label: FANBOYS conjunction
sentences.note: It joins two clauses inside one sentence, with a comma before it.

sentences.t: Because the bus was late, we walked.
sentences.label: Subordinating conjunction
sentences.note: It starts a subordinate clause. Comma when it comes first.

sentences.t: The bus was late. Therefore, we walked.
sentences.label: Transition
sentences.note: It starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon), with a comma after it.

spot.takeaway: **FANBOYS** (, but) · **subordinators** (because, although, when) · **transitions** (however, therefore, in addition). They look alike in meaning but **punctuate differently**.

practice.q: Which kind of linking word is it?
practice.why: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. Subordinators start a subordinate clause. Transitions start a new sentence.

help.nudge: Is it one of the seven FANBOYS words? If not, can it start a clause like “because…”?
help.rule: FANBOYS · subordinators (because, although, when, if) · transitions (however, therefore, moreover).
help.worked: “However” is not in FANBOYS, and it can’t start a subordinate clause, so it is a transition.

practice.q: Which sentence is a comma splice?
options: The bus was late, so we walked.
The bus was late, therefore we walked.
The bus was late. Therefore, we walked.
The bus was late; therefore, we walked.
practice.why: Therefore is a transition, not a FANBOYS word, so a comma alone can’t join the sentences.

help.nudge: Which linking word is NOT in FANBOYS?
help.rule: A comma alone can join sentences only with a FANBOYS word.
help.worked: “so” is in FANBOYS (fine). “therefore” is a transition (a comma splice here).

variants.q: Which sentence is a comma splice?
options: I was tired, but I finished.
I was tired, however I finished.
I was tired. However, I finished.
I was tired; however, I finished.
variants.why: However is a transition, so a comma alone can’t join the sentences.

practice.q: Rewrite with although (a conjunction) instead of however.
practice.show: The exam was hard. However, I passed.
accept: Although the exam was hard, I passed.
I passed although the exam was hard.
practice.example: Although the exam was hard, I passed.
practice.why: Although joins the ideas in one sentence: a comma when it comes first, none when it comes second.

help.nudge: Make one sentence with “Although …,” at the start.
help.rule: Although + clause, + main clause.
help.worked: Although the exam was hard, I passed.

practice.q: Rewrite with a transition: “We were tired, so we went home.”
practice.show: We were tired, so we went home.
patterns: ^We were tired\. (Therefore|As a result|Consequently), we went home\.$
^We were tired; (therefore|as a result|consequently), we went home\.$
practice.example: We were tired. Therefore, we went home.
practice.why: A transition needs a full stop (or semicolon) before it and a comma after it.

help.nudge: Make two sentences. Use Therefore, / As a result, / Consequently, for the second.
help.rule: Sentence. Transition, sentence.
help.worked: We were tired. Therefore, we went home.

practice.q: Which pair has the same meaning?
practice.why: But and however both show contrast, but they are punctuated differently.

help.nudge: Which two words both show a difference?
help.rule: Because = cause; therefore = effect; so = effect; although = contrast.
help.worked: But and however both show contrast.

write.prompt: Say the same idea **three ways**: “The shop was closed. We went home.” Use a joining word, a subordinator and a transition.

checks.t: I used a FANBOYS word with a comma.
I used a subordinator (because, although, when…).
I used a transition with the right punctuation.

write.sample: The shop was closed, so we went home. We went home because the shop was closed. The shop was closed. Therefore, we went home.

3.9.goal: Use linking words where they help, and avoid putting one in every sentence.

spot.intro: Tap each version to see when linking words help, and when they get in the way.

sentences.t: First, I woke up. Then, I ate. Next, I left. After that, I walked. Finally, I arrived.
sentences.label: Too many
sentences.note: A linking word in every sentence feels mechanical.

sentences.t: I woke up and ate quickly. After that, I left home and walked to school, where I arrived at eight.
sentences.label: Better
sentences.note: Fewer linking words, with ideas joined inside sentences.

sentences.t: It was raining. We stayed inside.
sentences.label: No linking word needed
sentences.note: The cause-and-effect link is already clear.

spot.takeaway: Use linking words **where they help**, not in every sentence. **Vary** them, and let ideas link themselves when the connection is obvious.

practice.q: Which version is better?
options: First, I woke up. Then, I ate. Next, I left. After that, I walked. Finally, I arrived.
I woke up, ate breakfast and left. After that, I walked to school and arrived at eight.
I woke up. I ate. I left. I walked. I arrived.
I woke up, then I ate, then I left, then I walked, then I arrived.
practice.why: It uses a linking word once and joins ideas inside sentences.

help.nudge: Which version sounds natural, not mechanical?
help.rule: Mix joined sentences with a few linking words.
help.worked: Option 1 has a linking word in every sentence. Option 3 has none and is choppy. Option 2 is balanced.

options: First, I cooked. Then, I ate. Next, I cleaned. After that, I rested. Finally, I slept.
I cooked and ate dinner. After that, I cleaned the kitchen and rested before I slept.
I cooked. I ate. I cleaned. I rested. I slept.
I cooked, then I ate, then I cleaned, then I rested, then I slept.
variants.why: Balanced: a linking word once, ideas joined inside sentences.

practice.q: Rewrite to avoid repeating also.
practice.show: I also like tea. I also like coffee. I also like juice.
practice.example: I like tea, coffee and juice.
practice.why: Combine the items in one sentence. Many answers work.

help.nudge: Put the three drinks in one list, with no repeated also.
help.rule: Join a list of items in one sentence.
help.worked: I like tea, coffee and juice.

practice.q: Which sentence shows the connection WITHOUT a linking word?
options: It was raining. We stayed inside.
It was raining. Moreover, we stayed inside.
It was raining. In contrast, we stayed inside.
It was raining. For example, we stayed inside.
practice.why: The cause and result are clear already. Moreover and in contrast would change the meaning.

help.nudge: Which version doesn’t need an extra word to make sense?
help.rule: If the link is obvious, you can leave the linking word out.
help.worked: Rain → staying inside: the cause and effect are obvious.

practice.q: How often should you use linking words?
options: Where they help the reader follow your ideas
Only at the start of paragraphs
practice.why: They are tools. Use them when they make the connection clearer.

help.nudge: Think about the reader.
help.rule: Use linking words where they help, not everywhere.
help.worked: Too many tire the reader; none can leave ideas disconnected.

practice.q: Rewrite as one smoother sentence without extra linking words.
practice.show: First, I made tea. Then, I made toast. Next, I ate breakfast.
practice.example: I made tea and toast and ate breakfast.
practice.why: Many answers work. Join the actions in one sentence without First / Then / Next.

help.nudge: Join the three actions with and, and drop First / Then / Next.
help.rule: A compound verb can join several actions.
help.worked: I made tea and toast and ate breakfast.

write.prompt: Write **a short paragraph (4–5 sentences)** about your weekend. Use linking words only where they help: at least two, but not in every sentence.

checks.t: I used at least two different linking words.
I did not put a linking word in every sentence.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: On Saturday, I visited my grandparents. We cooked lunch together, and we talked for hours. After that, I helped my grandfather in the garden. It was a quiet day, but I enjoyed it.

3.10.goal: Show that you can choose and punctuate linking words in a short paragraph.

write.prompt: Write a paragraph (5–6 sentences) about a change in your life. Use at least **four different linking words** from this stage (addition, contrast, cause and effect, example, sequence).
write.placeholder: A big change in my life was …

checks.t: I used at least four different linking words.
The punctuation around each linking word is correct.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: A big change in my life was moving to a new city. At first, I felt lonely because I did not know anyone. However, I joined a sports club. As a result, I made many friends, and I felt at home. In addition, I discovered new hobbies such as cycling. Overall, the move was a good decision.

add.label: Adding words
add.improve: Use also, in addition, moreover to add a point, with a comma after a starting transition.

contrast.label: Contrast words
contrast.improve: Contrast words (but, however, although, whereas) show a difference.

cause.label: Cause and effect
cause.good: You show cause and effect clearly.
cause.improve: Cause: because, since. Effect: so, therefore, as a result. Because of + noun.

example.label: Giving examples
example.improve: For example, + comma starts a sentence. Such as / including work inside a sentence.

sequence.label: Sequence words
sequence.good: You show the order of events well.
sequence.improve: Use first, next, then, after that, finally with a comma.

concl.label: Conclusion words
concl.improve: Use in conclusion, to sum up, overall only at the end, with a comma.

lpunct.label: Punctuating linking words
lpunct.improve: Transitions need a full stop or semicolon before and a comma after.

ctrans.label: Conjunctions and transitions
ctrans.improve: FANBOYS and subordinators join clauses; transitions start a new sentence.

overuse.label: Not overusing linking words
overuse.good: You use linking words with care.
overuse.improve: Use linking words where they help, not in every sentence.
